narrative:
The model predicted a 67.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year performance in law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile compared to an average of sixth decile among accepted students signaled that you started your legal studies at a significant disadvantage relative to your peers. Your third-year performance was the third most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure, as you ranked in the second decile while successful applicants averaged near the sixth.

Working in the opposite direction, your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential feature and pulled the prediction toward passing. At 3.40 it stood noticeably above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance about your overall academic ability.

Taken together, the early law-school struggles outweighed your solid college record and raised the predicted risk of bar failure high enough to prevent admission. 

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your foundational legal skills before retaking the exam or reapplying. Consider targeted bar-prep courses, additional coursework, or a structured study plan that addresses the specific areas where your early performance lagged. Many students successfully improve their trajectory with deliberate effort in these areas.
